messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 49

She was making her last delivery of the night, a routine drop-off at an apartment complex on the edge of town. The address was a second-floor unit, and she parked her sedan under a flickering streetlight, leaving the engine running and the hazard lights on. It had been a long shift—twelve hours of navigating traffic, carrying takeout bags, and forcing a smile for customers who often didn’t look at her face. She was tired. The kind of tired that makes your bones ache and your thoughts go slow.

That was six months ago.

Now, she tells herself it was just a few seconds. A man came out from between two buildings, his face obscured by a hood. He grabbed her arm when she stepped out of the car with the food bag. He had a knife—small, dull-looking, but she saw the blade catch the light. “Give me your phone. Your wallet. Now.” She didn’t scream. She just handed over everything. Her phone, her wallet, the bag of food. He shoved her back against the car door and ran. She stood there for what felt like ten minutes, heart hammering, before she got back in the car and drove straight home. She didn’t call the police until the next morning.

She still delivers food, because she needs the money. But everything is different now. She only works day shifts, though even daylight feels unsafe. Her mother, a widow who she lives with, tells her she is being dramatic. “You were not hurt. You still have your life. Move on.” So she does not talk about it at home. She tries to smile when her mother asks why she’s jumpy.

In the car, she checks every street corner three times before she pulls over. She locks the doors as soon as she sits down. She keeps a small can of pepper spray in the cup holder, even though it’s not legal for her to carry it. When she has a delivery to a building with an alley near the entrance, she circles the block twice, then parks a block away and walks with her keys between her fingers. She has not told her manager about the mugging. She is afraid they will fire her for being a liability.

At night, she cannot sleep. She lies awake listening for footsteps outside her bedroom window. Every car door slamming makes her chest tighten. She has lost eight pounds because eating feels like a chore—her stomach clenches every time she sits down to a meal. Her mother complains that she is “wasting away,” but she doesn’t know how to explain that she can still taste her own saliva from that night, the metallic sour, the way her throat closed up.

She gave a statement to the police, but they never found the man. Sometimes she sees him in other people—a guy at the gas station with the same slouched shoulders, a customer who reaches too quickly for the bag. Her heart races, her palms sweat, and she has to sit on the curb until the world stops spinning. She stopped seeing her few friends because she cannot sit still in a cafe for more than twenty minutes without scanning every face, every exit.

The PCL-5 she filled out at a free clinic lasted two weeks ago just to “check in.” She scored 49. She did not know what that meant, but the therapist who gave it to her seemed concerned. The therapist asked if she wanted to come back. She said yes, but she hasn’t called. She isn’t sure she deserves to take up time when others have it worse.
